1366.title: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1366.hook: one diner reaching for seconds, another pushing the plate away and proud of it: Lal Ded has a word for both, and a door that opens in between
1366.carry: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1366.tomorrow: in their own words where they exist
1366.howItsDone: Lal Ded's vakhs, this one among them, are recited and sung in Kashmiri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded's two strips of cloth, knotted for every insult and every bow, weighed the same at evening.
screen: `LAL DED.`

segments.voice: Two people at the same table. One keeps reaching for seconds, then thirds, long after hunger has gone. The other pushes the plate away half full, and feels a little glow of being better than the first. Neither would call what they're doing spiritual. Lal Ded would. She has a short saying about food that catches both diners at once. It doesn't scold one and praise the other. It finds a problem with each, and then it points to a door.
screen: `ONE DINER REACHES FOR MORE.` → `ONE PUSHES THE PLATE AWAY.` → `A SAYING THAT CATCHES BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. Eat and eat, and you'll get nowhere. Stop eating, and you'll grow proud. Eat in measure, and you'll become even, and the bolted doors will open. The first line is easy to hear: overeating gets you nowhere. The second has the sting. Not eating doesn't make you holy. It can make you proud. Lal Ded had lived through hunger, if the story of the stone under the rice is true, and she wandered as a seeker. Of all people, she could have praised the hard road. Instead she warns that it has its own trap: being pleased with yourself for how little you need. Then the middle: eat in measure. What that brings, she says, is evenness, and out of evenness the bolted doors swing open. She doesn't say which doors. Some readers hear the doors within, the ones her teacher's one word pointed to. The Bhagavad Gita has a neighbor to this saying, in paraphrase: yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all, nor for the one who sleeps too much or too little. Lal Ded puts it in her own Kashmiri, at a kitchen table. A last day with her, then, and a plate, neither heaped nor empty. Like her rope and her unbaked cup, a small, homely picture, and this one ends at a door.
screen: `TOO MUCH GETS YOU NOWHERE` · `TOO LITTLE MAKES YOU PROUD` · `IN MEASURE, THE DOORS OPEN` · `A PLATE THAT ENDS AT A DOOR`

segments.voice: Take one breath that's too big, filling all the way, and let it go; then one too small, barely there, and let it go. Then let the breath find its own size, not grabbing, not holding back, and when the mind reaches for more or pulls away, come back to the middle. If you pray, you can rest in that evenness before God.
Lal Ded. The poet who said eating too much gets you nowhere, not eating makes you proud, and eating in measure opens the bolted doors. Today's word.
screen: `LAL DED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Lal Ded, a season of the tradition's women. Not heaped, not empty: in measure. Rest well.

1367.title: in their own words where they exist
1367.word: in their own words where they exist
1367.hook: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off: the warning Gargi got in a king's hall, and the two questions she came back with
1367.carry: in their own words where they exist
1367.tomorrow: in their own words where they exist
1367.howItsDone: Gargi's questions are read and studied wherever the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is taught.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Lal Ded: too much gets you nowhere, too little makes you proud, and in measure the doors open.
screen: `LAL DED.`

segments.voice: Don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. That's a line from an Upanishad, said in a king's hall in front of learned men, to a woman who wouldn't stop asking questions. Her name is Gargi, and you first met her back in year two. She falls silent. And later, in the same debate, she stands up again. Akka and Lalla left sayings of their own. Other women's words didn't survive at all. And some, like Gargi's, speak inside a text that's mostly about someone else. Where their words exist, we listen.
screen: `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH.` → `A WOMAN WHO KEEPS ASKING.` → `HER WORDS INSIDE ANOTHER STORY.`

segments.voice: The text is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. King Janaka of Videha has called the wise to his court, and the sage Yajnavalkya is answering all comers. Gargi steps forward. Her question, in paraphrase: all this world is woven back and forth on water, like threads on a loom. So on what is water woven? On wind, he says. And wind? On the sky. Layer after layer, each answer becomes her next question. Then Yajnavalkya stops her: Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off; you're asking too far about a deity not to be asked about like this. And she falls silent. It's easy to stop there, as if she lost. The text doesn't. After another sage has questioned him and been answered, she rises again and tells the assembly: I will ask him two questions. If he can answer them, none of you will beat him. The Upanishad pictures her coming at him like a warrior from Kashi or Videha, stringing an unstrung bow, taking up two arrows that can pierce. Her questions: that which is above the sky and below the earth, and between them, past, present and future, on what is it woven? In space, he answers. And space, on what is that woven? This time the answer goes deeper than wind and water, to the imperishable, which sees and is not seen. Gargi tells the assembly none of them will beat him. Notice what carries the debate to its deepest answer. Not only his replies. Her questions.
screen: `A DEBATE IN KING JANAKA'S HALL` · `ON WHAT IS IT WOVEN?` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH` · `TWO ARROWS, TWO QUESTIONS`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, a cup, a hand, the floor, and ask quietly: what holds this up? Let an answer come, then ask the same of that answer. When you reach the place where no answer comes, don't push; rest there in the question, the way Gargi did when she fell silent, and if you pray, rest there before God.
In their own words, where they exist: Gargi, warned not to ask too much, who came back with two questions like arrows. Today's word.

1368.title: in their own words where they exist
1368.word: in their own words where they exist
1368.hook: a husband about to leave home offers to settle his property, and his wife answers with a question: Maitreyi in the Upanishad
1368.carry: in their own words where they exist
1368.tomorrow: in their own words where they exist
1368.howItsDone: The dialogue of Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi is read and taught as part of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi, warned not to ask too much, came back with two questions like arrows.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: A man is about to leave home for good, to live as a wandering seeker. Before he goes, he does the responsible thing: he sits down with his wife to settle the property, so that she and his other wife will be provided for. The will, the house, the money. His wife listens. Then, instead of asking how much, she asks something else entirely. The man is Yajnavalkya again, the sage Gargi questioned. The wife is Maitreyi, whom you first met in year one.
screen: `A MAN ABOUT TO LEAVE HOME.` → `THE TALK ABOUT THE PROPERTY.` → `MAITREYI ASKS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi he's about to leave this life at home, and wants to make a settlement between her and Katyayani, his other wife. Maitreyi answers, in paraphrase: sir, if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, would I become immortal by it? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich; there's no hope of immortality through wealth. Then her line: what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. She isn't refusing to be provided for. She's refusing to let the property be the whole conversation. If he's leaving to seek what doesn't die, she wants that, not a share of what does. Notice how he answers. The text has him say she is truly dear to him, and speaks dear words. Then he sits with her and teaches. A husband is dear, he says, not for the husband's own sake, but for the sake of the Self. A wife, children, wealth, the world itself: all dear for the sake of the Self. It's the Self that must be seen, heard, thought on, and meditated upon. So a teaching on the Self is set down as an answer to a wife's question at the edge of a goodbye. Maitreyi's words are few. But they're hers, and without them the teaching has no door to come through.
screen: `THE TALK ABOUT THE PROPERTY` · `WOULD WEALTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` · `WHAT WOULD I DO WITH IT?` · `DEAR FOR THE SAKE OF THE SELF`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're working toward or wanting right now, a purchase, a promotion, a result, and hold it gently. Ask Maitreyi's question of it, without judging: what would I do with this? Let the honest answer come, then turn toward whatever feels deeper than the thing itself and rest there; if you pray, bring that deeper want before God.
In their own words, where they exist. Today, Maitreyi, offered a share of the property, asking what she would do with what can't make her immortal. Today's word.

1369.title: in their own words where they exist
1369.word: in their own words where they exist
1369.hook: a poet signs her hymns not with a title but as a ghoul of the cremation ground: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, in her own words
1369.carry: in their own words where they exist
1369.howItsDone: Tamil Shaivas honor Karaikkal Ammaiyar among the Nayanars; her hymns are sung as part of the Tirumurai, and her image is found in Shiva temples, seated near the dancing Shiva.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maitreyi, offered a share of the property, asked what she'd do with what can't make her immortal.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: At the end of a hymn, the poet signs her name. Some Tamil hymns close this way, with the singer's name set into the last verse. This poet doesn't sign as a saint, or a lady, or a devotee. She signs as a pey, a ghoul, the kind of gaunt spirit said to haunt the burning grounds. The pey of Karaikkal. Earlier on this path we met her at her own door, giving away a mango. Today, the name she gave herself.
screen: `A POET SIGNS HER NAME.` → `NOT A SAINT: A GHOUL.` → `THE PEY OF KARAIKKAL.`

segments.voice: Her tradition's story is in the Periya Puranam, the book of the lives of the Shaiva saints. Her name was Punitavati, a merchant's wife in Karaikkal. After the mango, her husband grew afraid of her and left. So she asked Shiva to take away the beauty she had kept for him, and give her the body of a pey instead, bones and sinew, fit only for praising him. The story says she went to Shiva's mountain walking on her hands, so her feet wouldn't touch its holy ground, and that Shiva, seeing her, called her Mother. So she's known as Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. Now her own words, in paraphrase. Her hymns picture Shiva dancing at night in the cremation ground, with flames, ash and owls, and ghouls dancing around him. Among them is the singer herself: in the closing verse she names herself the pey of Karaikkal, the one who sings these words. In another poem she says that from the time she was born and learned to speak, her love was for his feet. So two names sit side by side. Mother is the name the story says Shiva gave her. Ghoul is the name she gave herself. She didn't hide the bones; she signed with them. Her hymns are kept in the Tirumurai, the sacred collection that holds the Tevaram. And that closes this season: Sita, Draupadi, Kunti, Gandhari, Savitri, Damayanti and Shakuntala in the epics; Andal, Mirabai, Akka and Lalla in the songs; Gargi and Maitreyi in the Upanishad; and a woman who chose her own strange name.
screen: `PUNITAVATI ASKS FOR A NEW BODY` · `SHIVA CALLS HER MOTHER` · `SHE SIGNS AS THE PEY OF KARAIKKAL` · `A SEASON OF WOMEN, CLOSED`

segments.voice: Notice the names other people use for you, a title, a role, a nickname, and let them pass one at a time. Then ask quietly: if I signed a song about what I love most, what would I call myself? Don't polish it, let it be strange if it's strange, and rest with it; if you pray, you can offer that name to God.
In their own words, where they exist: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, called Mother in the story, who signed her hymns as the pey of Karaikkal. Today's word.

1370.title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
1370.hook: a locked room in a temple, a king outside the door, and palm leaves half eaten by ants: how tradition says the Tevaram came back
1370.howItsDone: In Tamil Shaiva temples, singers called oduvars sing hymns from the Tevaram during worship.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a season with Karaikkal Ammaiyar, who signed her hymns as the pey of Karaikkal. Her songs sit beside the Tevaram, where we go today.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: A sealed door in the great temple at Chidambaram, the temple of Shiva as the dancer. Behind it, tradition says, lies a room long left unopened. Outside stands a Chola king. He has heard a few verses of the old Tamil hymns to Shiva sung at his court, and he wants the rest. The priests won't open the door. Only the singers who made these hymns, they say, can open it, and those singers are long gone. A new part of the path begins here: the regional traditions, starting in the Tamil south.
screen: `A SEALED DOOR AT CHIDAMBARAM.` → `A KING WHO WANTS THE HYMNS.` → `ONLY THE SINGERS CAN OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, as tradition tells it, in paraphrase. If only the saints can open the door, he'll bring the saints. He has images of the three singers, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, carried through the streets in procession and set before the room. The door opens. Inside are the palm leaves the hymns were written on, much of them eaten away by white ants. The king is heartbroken. Then, the story says, a voice is heard: what this age needs has been kept. A learned devotee, Nambi Andar Nambi, gathers what survives and sets it in order, and the hymns are sung again. That gathering is the Tevaram, at the heart of the Tirumurai, the sacred collection of Tamil Shaiva hymns. The story is about loss as much as rescue. It doesn't pretend nothing was lost; the ants got there first, and still, what was needed remained. And look at the hymns themselves. They are in Tamil, not Sanskrit, and they're tied to places. A hymn praises the Shiva of this town, by this river, in this grove, with this temple tank. The singers walked from shrine to shrine and sang each one. Tamil Shaivism is a faith with a map in its scripture. And in the story, the key to the room was the singers themselves: their words could only be opened by their presence. That's the ground a regional tradition stands on: Shiva, worshiped in a particular language, in particular places, through particular voices.
screen: `THE SAINTS CARRIED TO THE DOOR` · `PALM LEAVES EATEN BY ANTS` · `WHAT THIS AGE NEEDS WAS KEPT` · `HYMNS WITH A MAP INSIDE`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that came to you only in part: a grandmother's recipe half remembered, a few words of a language, a song you know only the chorus of, a faith handed to you in pieces. Don't grieve the missing parts for now; hold what remains, and let it be enough to sit with. If you pray, you can give thanks for what was kept.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram: the hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, sung place by place and, tradition says, rescued from a sealed room at Chidambaram. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Palm leaves, white ants, and songs sung again. Until tomorrow.

1371.title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
1371.hook: a wedding stopped by an old man waving a deed that says the groom is his slave: how Sundarar's first hymn began with an insult
1371.howItsDone: Tamil Shaivas sing Sundarar's hymns as part of the Tevaram in temple worship, and his story is told from the Periya Puranam.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sealed room at Chidambaram, palm leaves eaten by ants, and what this age needs, kept: the Tevaram.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM.`

segments.voice: The wedding is under way. The groom is a handsome young man named Arurar, the families are gathered, the rites have begun. Then an old Brahmin pushes through the crowd, holding up a palm-leaf deed. This young man, he announces, is my slave. His grandfather signed him over to me, him and all his line. The groom loses his temper, calls the old man a madman, and tears the deed to pieces. That insult, the story says, is how one of the Tevaram's three singers found his first word.
screen: `A WEDDING UNDER WAY.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH A DEED.` → `YOU MADMAN.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The old man isn't put off. That was only a copy, he says; the original is kept in his own town. So the wedding party follows him there, and before the village elders he produces the deed. They compare the handwriting with the grandfather's. It matches. The groom is bound. Then the old man leads them toward the temple, walks inside, and vanishes. It was Shiva. And Shiva speaks to the young man: you called me a madman, so sing of me, and begin with that word. The young man, known ever after as Sundarar, opens his first hymn with it. In paraphrase: madman, wearing the crescent moon in your hair. The name he shouted in anger becomes praise. Shiva in this story doesn't wait for good manners. He takes the insult and hands it back as a first line. And look at the deed. In Tamil Shaivism devotees are called adiyar, the Lord's servants. Sundarar's whole calling begins with a document saying exactly that: he belongs to someone. The story says he spent his life singing from temple to temple, and the tradition gives him a second title too, the Lord's friend. Servant and friend, in one man. One more thing: the wedding didn't happen. That's a hard ending for a bride, and the story doesn't hide it. Tomorrow, an older singer, and a king who summons him.
screen: `THE DEED IS REAL` · `THE OLD MAN WAS SHIVA` · `BEGIN WITH THAT WORD: MADMAN` · `SERVANT AND FRIEND`

1372.title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
1372.hook: a king summons a temple singer, and Appar sends back a song instead
1372.howItsDone: In Tamil Shaiva temples, singers called oduvars sing hymns of the Tevaram, including Appar's, during worship, and Appar is often shown in images carrying his small hoe.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sundarar began his first hymn with the word he shouted at his wedding: madman. A week from Lal Ded in Kashmir to the Tamil south.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM.`

segments.voice: A messenger arrives with an order from the king: come to court. The man being summoned is a singer of Shiva, carrying a small hoe, the kind used to pull grass from between the stones of a temple courtyard. The stories call him Appar. Then, instead of packing a bag, he answers with a song. Its opening, in paraphrase: we are subjects of no one, and we do not fear death. The messenger goes back carrying a hymn instead of a prisoner.
screen: `AN ORDER FROM THE KING.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH A HOE.` → `A SONG SENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Appar's life is told in the Periya Puranam, the book of the lives of the Shaiva saints. It says he spent a long time on another path and then came home to Shiva, and that the king was angry about it. So the order is a threat, not an invitation. The song, in paraphrase: we are no one's subjects, we do not fear death, we will not suffer in hell, we do not tremble, we know no sickness, we bow to no one, because we belong to the Lord. This isn't a protest against kings in general. It's a statement about ownership. If his whole life belongs to Shiva, there's no room left for a second master. Then look at the hoe. The man who bows to no king spends his days on his knees, pulling weeds from temple stones so others can walk there barefoot. Free of the palace, and a servant of the courtyard, in the same body. Tradition says the king had him tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the sea, and that Appar sang the five syllables, namah shivaya, and the stone floated him to shore. Some readers take that as a plain miracle; others hear a picture of what the name of Shiva can hold up. Either way, he carries into the water not an argument, but a name. On an ordinary day, the song isn't telling anyone to ignore their boss. It asks a quieter question: under all the voices that summon you, which one do you finally answer to?
screen: `A SUMMONS THAT IS A THREAT` · `SUBJECTS OF NO ONE` · `A HOE FOR THE TEMPLE STONES` · `THE STONE THAT FLOATED`
